lesson.title: Exponential Population Growth: The Math Behind Unchecked Growth
lesson.summary: Exponential population growth occurs when a population increases by a constant proportion each time period under unlimited resources, producing an accelerating, J-shaped growth curve described by the equation dN/dt = rN.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters covered population density and dispersion patterns, both of which describe a population at a single point in time. This chapter turns to how a population's size changes over time, starting with the simplest case: what happens when growth is essentially unrestricted because resources are abundant relative to the population's current size.

Exponential growth describes a population that increases by a constant proportion each time period, which produces an accelerating increase in absolute numbers over time, since that constant proportional growth rate is applied to an ever larger starting population at each step. Plotted on a graph of population size against time, exponential growth traces a curve that starts out nearly flat and then sweeps sharply upward, often described as J-shaped.

This relationship is captured by the equation dN divided by dt equals r times N, usually written dN/dt = rN. Here, N is the population size, t is time, dN/dt is the instantaneous rate of change in population size with respect to time, and r is the per capita rate of increase, sometimes called the intrinsic rate of increase, representing births minus deaths per individual per unit of time (this simplified version assumes no immigration or emigration). The intuition behind the equation is straightforward: the larger the population already is, the more new individuals it adds per unit of time, even if the per capita rate r itself stays exactly the same, which is the compounding quality that makes exponential growth accelerate.

Solving that equation over time gives the more directly useful form N sub t equals N sub 0 times e raised to the power of r times t, usually written N_t = N_0 * e^(rt), where N_0 is the population size at the starting time, N_t is the population size at time t, and e is the base of the natural logarithm, approximately 2.71828. Here is a fully worked example. Suppose a population starts at N_0 = 100 individuals with a per capita growth rate of r = 0.5 per year (a 50 percent per capita increase per year). After t = 4 years, N_t = 100 times e raised to the power of (0.5 times 4), which is 100 times e squared. Since e squared is approximately 7.389, N_t is approximately 100 times 7.389, or about 739 individuals, more than seven times the starting population in just four years. It is also worth noticing that the instantaneous growth rate itself grows as the population grows: at the very start, dN/dt = rN = 0.5 times 100, or 50 individuals added per year at that instant, but by year four, with N at about 739, the instantaneous rate has climbed to roughly 0.5 times 739, or about 370 individuals per year. The rate of growth is not constant in absolute terms, even though the per capita rate r is constant, which is precisely what produces the accelerating J-shaped curve.

Exponential growth requires conditions where resources, both abiotic factors like space and nutrients and biotic factors like low predation or competition, are effectively unlimited relative to the population's current size. Real examples include bacteria introduced into a fresh, nutrient rich culture medium, an invasive species introduced into a new environment with no established predators or competitors, or a population rebounding into a habitat that remains far below its historical numbers.

No natural population, however, sustains exponential growth indefinitely, since resources are always finite in the real world. This model should be understood as a useful starting idealization rather than a description of how populations actually behave over the long run. As a population grows, density dependent factors, the abiotic and biotic pressures discussed in earlier chapters, typically become more significant and slow the growth rate down, a more realistic pattern that builds directly on the concepts introduced here but is not covered in full in this chapter.
